newsitem.title: UK: Governments ignoring plight of refugees - Amnesty.
newsitem.headline: Governments ignoring plight of refugees - Amnesty.

text.p: Amnesty International accused governments around the world on Wednesday of failing to take responsibility for the tides of refugees fleeing armed conflicts and human rights abuses.
The number of refugees seeking protection from human violations had nearly doubled to 15 million in the past decade, and the international system to protect them was in crisis.
"The growing number of refugees is neither a temporary problem nor a random product of chance events," the London-based human rights group said its annual report.
"It is the predictable consequence of human rights crises throughout the world."
In 1996, governments triggered refugee flows by carrying out human rights abuses at home, and directly and indirectly fuelling conflict in places like central Africa, Afghanistan and Colombia.

At the same time, Amnesty said more and more governments worldwide had refused to protect millions of refugees fleeing terror. In Africa alone there are five million refugees and at least 16 million internally displaced people.
"They closed their borders and forcibly returned thousands of refugees to dangerous situations where their safety was at risk," said Amnesty's Secretary General, Pierre Sane.
Developed countries were worsening the plight of refugees by tightening their asylum policies. Many countries traditionally welcoming to refugees, such as Iran, had hardened their attitudes.
The report, covering human rights abuses in 151 countries last year, detailed thousands of extrajudicial executions or possible extrajudicial executions in at least 69 countries.
Amnesty, which opposes capital punishment, said thousands more legally-sanctioned executions took place in at least 41 countries.
Prisoners of conscience were detained in at least 94 countries. Amnesty recorded cases of torture or ill-treatment in at least 124 countries and "disappearances" in at least 39.
But the report concentrated on the growing problem of refugees, not only in central Africa but also in Europe, Asia and the Middle East.
Many refugee crises were foreseen, as in Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia, but the international community had taken little heed, Amnesty said.

"Yet again, during 1996, the standard government response has been to treat the symptoms, not the cause," said Sane. "There can be no long-term solution to refugee flows until the underlying reason -- the fear of human rights abuses -- is tackled."
States pay lip service to protecting refugees but their political will is dwindling along with their commitment to offering asylum.
"The international regime that is supposed to protect refugees is in crisis," the report said.

"The U.N. Refugee Convention and its Protocol, which was designed to protect refugees fleeing persecution, often prove inadequate because many situations faced by refugees today are deemed to fall outside their terms."

Developed countries are increasingly returning individuals forcibly to countries where their lives are threatened, often after blocking access to refugees through bureaucratic means and tighter border controls.
"Amnesty International calls on governments to ensure that their asylum procedures meet minimum international standards of fairness, impartiality and thoroughness," the report said.

So-called "southern" or less-developed countries are increasingly turning against refugees. There is no secure mechanism by which these countries can gain outside assistance to care for them. "To make matters worse, aid is often pledged and then not given," Amnesty said.

"They (southern countries) are coercing refugees to return to their countries of origin, using measures which include cutting food supplies and, as was the case in the mass expulsions of Rwandese refugees from Tanzania in December, the use of force."
